title: XGBoost, LightGBM & CatBoost
tagline: The three production-grade gradient boosting libraries that actually win competitions.
what_it_is: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost are optimized, industrial-strength implementations of gradient boosting. They add engineering improvements — regularization, faster tree-building, smarter handling of missing values and categorical features — on top of the core gradient boosting idea, making them fast enough and accurate enough for real production systems.
key_points: All three implement gradient boosting on decision trees — the differences are in speed, memory, and default handling of tricky data.
XGBoost added built-in L1/L2 regularization and efficient handling of missing values, becoming the early competition standard.
LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise instead of level-wise, making it much faster on large datasets.
CatBoost handles categorical features natively without manual encoding, and reduces a bias called 'prediction shift.'
All three support early stopping, feature importance, and GPU acceleration.
why_it_exists: Vanilla gradient boosting is powerful but slow and memory-hungry on real-world, large, messy datasets with missing values and categorical columns. These libraries exist to make gradient boosting practical at production scale — faster training, better defaults, and less manual preprocessing.
intuition: If gradient boosting is the recipe, these libraries are three different professional kitchens that all cook the same dish — but one is optimized for speed (LightGBM), one is the reliable industry-standard kitchen everyone learned on (XGBoost), and one is built to handle a messier pantry of ingredients without extra prep work (CatBoost's native categorical handling).
when_to_use: Use XGBoost as a safe, well-documented default for tabular problems, especially in interviews and competitions.
Use LightGBM when you have a very large dataset and training speed matters.
Use CatBoost when your data has many categorical columns and you want to skip manual encoding.
when_not_to_use: Do not reach for these on small datasets (a few hundred rows) — simpler models often generalize just as well with less tuning risk.
Do not use them on raw unstructured data (images, audio, free text) without prior feature extraction.
Do not skip hyperparameter tuning and expect defaults to be optimal — these models are sensitive to settings like max_depth and learning_rate.
common_mistakes: Blindly picking XGBoost out of habit even when LightGBM would train faster on a huge dataset.
One-hot encoding categorical variables before feeding them into CatBoost — defeats its main advantage.
Not monitoring validation loss with early stopping, leading to overfit models that look great on training data only.
ds_usage: The default choice for tabular ML in industry and competitions — used for fraud detection, pricing models, recommendation ranking, and churn prediction wherever data comes as structured rows and columns.
